{{Short description|Bias which mixes cause and effect}}{{AI-generated|date=July 2026}}

In [[statistics]] and [[machine learning]], '''temporal bias''' is an error or distortion in reasoning, [[data analysis]], or [[predictive modeling]] that occurs when the timing of events or data collection is handled improperly or ignored.<ref name="Yuan2021">Yuan, William, et al. [https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-021-21390-2 "Temporal bias in case-control design: preventing reliable predictions of the future."] ''Nature Communications'' 12.1 (2021): 1107.</ref><ref name="Savitz2023">Savitz, David A., and Gregory A. Wellenius. [https://doi.org/10.1093/aje/kwac037 "Can Cross-Sectional Studies Contribute to Causal Inference? It Depends."] ''American Journal of Epidemiology'' 192.4 (2023): 514-516.</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Taş |first1=Pelin Gülüm |last2=Maknoon |first2=Yousef |last3=Rezaei |first3=Jafar |date=2026-01-20 |title=Time's Influence: A Systematic Review of Biases in Intertemporal Decision-Making |url=https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-psych-091924-040158 |journal=Annual Review of Psychology |language=en |volume=77 |issue=77 |pages=223–254 |doi=10.1146/annurev-psych-091924-040158 |pmid=40829785 |issn=0066-4308|doi-access=free }}</ref> The concept is recognized across different disciplines, including [[epidemiology]], machine learning, and [[cognitive psychology]].<ref name="Yuan2021" /><ref name=":0" /><ref name="Pendlebury2019">{{Cite journal |last1=Pendlebury |first1=Feargus |last2=Pierazzi |first2=Fabio |last3=Jordaney |first3=Roberto |last4=Kinder |first4=Johannes |last5=Cavallaro |first5=Lorenzo |date=2019 |title=TESSERACT: Eliminating Experimental Bias in Malware Classification across Space and Time |url=https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity19/presentation/pendlebury |journal=[[USENIX]] |language=en |pages=729–746 |isbn=978-1-939133-06-9}}</ref><ref name="McGuire2013">McGuire, Joseph T., and Joseph W. Kable. [https://doi.org/10.1037/a0031910 "Rational temporal predictions can underlie apparent failures to delay gratification."] ''Psychological Review'' 120.2 (2013): 395.</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Koterov |first1=A. N. |last2=Ushenkova |first2=L. N. |last3=Biryukov |first3=A. P. |date=2020-12-01 |title=Hill's Temporality Criterion: Reverse Causation and Its Radiation Aspect |url=https://doi.org/10.1134/S1062359020120031 |journal=Biology Bulletin |language=en |volume=47 |issue=12 |pages=1577–1609 |doi=10.1134/S1062359020120031 |bibcode=2020BioBu..47.1577K |issn=1608-3059|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Its exact definition and implications may vary by field.<ref name="Yuan2021" /><ref name=":0" /><ref name="McGuire2013" />

== Causal inference ==
In [[epidemiology]], temporal bias occurs when a study design cannot establish the correct sequence of events between an exposure and an outcome.<ref name="Savitz2023"/><ref name=":0" /> It is sometimes referred to as temporal ambiguity or [[reverse causation]].<ref name="Savitz2023"/><ref name=":0" /> Establishing temporality is a major criterion for [[causal inference]].<ref name="Savitz2023"/><ref name=":0" />

This bias is common in observational research, such as [[cross-sectional study|cross-sectional studies]], where variables are measured simultaneously at a single point in time.<ref name="Savitz2023"/><ref name=":0" /><ref name="Fairchild2024">Fairchild, Amanda J., et al. [https://doi.org/10.1037/met0000628 "A sensitivity analysis for temporal bias in cross-sectional mediation."] ''Psychological Methods'' 29.1 (2024): 101-118.</ref> For example, if a cross-sectional study finds an association between education level and health outcomes, researchers may be unable to determine whether lower education led to poor health or if poor health led to lower education.<ref name="Yuan2021" /><ref name="Savitz2023"/><ref name="Fairchild2024"/> Temporal bias can also occur in [[case-control study|case-control studies]] when the time period from which the data is drawn does not accurately represent the timeline clinicians experience during the actual diagnostic process.<ref name="Yuan2021"/> This misalignment can also inflate the predictive power of variables that appear close to the time of an outcome, which will undermine the reliability of the study's predictions.<ref name="Yuan2021"/>

A form of temporal bias is [[spurious correlation]] resulting from time, where non-causal associations in data may appear as the result of shared connections to time.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Yule |first=G. Udny |date=1926 |title=Why do we Sometimes get Nonsense-Correlations between Time-Series?--A Study in Sampling and the Nature of Time-Series |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2341482 |journal=Journal of the Royal Statistical Society |volume=89 |issue=1 |pages=1–63 |doi=10.2307/2341482 |jstor=2341482 |issn=0952-8385|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Artificial intelligence ==
In [[machine learning]] and [[artificial intelligence]], temporal bias can manifest as experimental evaluation errors or as historical bias within training data.<ref name="Pendlebury2019"/><ref name="IBMDataBias">IBM. [https://www.ibm.com/topics/data-bias "What is Data Bias?"] Retrieved 25 May 2026.</ref>

When evaluating models, temporal bias occurs if the training and testing datasets are randomly split without respecting the chronological order of the data.<ref name="Pendlebury2019"/> This incorrect time split allows the model to learn from future information that would not logically be available in a real-world deployment, leading to artificially inflated performance metrics. This may also indirectly lead to an ambiguous [[knowledge cutoff]].<ref name="Pendlebury2019"/><ref>{{Cite web |last=Colton |first=Emma |date=2023-06-28 |title=Can ChatGPT discuss current events? Chatbot has clear knowledge cutoff date |url=https://www.foxnews.com/tech/can-chatgpt-discuss-current-events-chatbot-knowledge-cutoff-date |access-date=2026-05-25 |website=Fox News |language=en-US}}</ref>

Additionally, temporal bias occurs when training data reflects historical inequalities or biases that existed during data collection, rather than the current context.<ref name="IBMDataBias"/> For example, an artificial intelligence hiring system trained on historical employment data may perpetuate past inequalities if certain demographics were historically underrepresented in high-level roles.<ref name="IBMDataBias"/>

== Human psychology ==
In [[cognitive psychology]], temporal biases may describe how human perception and decision-making are distorted by time.<ref name="McGuire2013"/><ref name="Tipples2011">Tipples, Jason. [https://doi.org/10.1037/a0022015 "When time stands still: fear-specific modulation of temporal bias due to threat."] ''Emotion'' 11.1 (2011): 74-80.</ref> A primary form is a bias towards the near future, where individuals overvalue immediate events and undervalue long term or past consequences, which influences their [[Delayed gratification|delay of gratification]].<ref name="McGuire2013"/>

Temporal bias also manifests as temporal distortion, where individuals inaccurately perceive the progression or duration of time based on emotional states.<ref name="Tipples2011"/> For example, studies have shown that fear-inducing stimuli may cause temporal overestimation, meaning individuals will perceive threatening events as lasting longer than they actually do due to emotion-specific temporal biases.<ref name="Tipples2011"/>
